title: Opening The Heart
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart's talk centered around the Heart Sutra, a Buddhist teaching that emphasizes the interconnectedness of all phenomena and the lack of a separate self. By exploring the concept of emptiness, which is central to the sutra, listeners can gain insight into how our perceptions of form, sensation, perception, and consciousness are not independent entities, but rather intertwined aspects of reality. This understanding can bring relief from suffering by dissolving the notion of a heavy burden or separate self, allowing us to experience life in a more authentic and liberated way.

sentences.text: Good evening, friends.
I hope you're well, and if you're not well, I hope you can bear it with equanimity.
I myself am enjoying the seasonal weather we're having here in Bellingham right now.
It feels like all four seasons can happen in a day: it can be nice and sunny, it can be foggy, it can rain, and then it's really cold at night.
Cold, wet, windy, sunny.
From white open sky to clouds so low I can touch them.
Yesterday and today were on the sunny side, which I truly love.
Nevertheless, I feel I was cheated out of it, because I got laid flat by a monster headache.
So in a way you will be cheated too, but not too much, I hope, because I couldn't write a coherent talk.
So I decided to give an old one.
I'm so sorry.
I really couldn't.
But I really like this one, so I think it's worthwhile to listen to it, especially if you haven't been here for a very long time.
I don't know how it was for you to come to the Zen Temple for the first time, or what your first impressions were.
I remember going up those dark stairs at the Freemason building on North State Street.
We chanted the Heart Sutra and the Enmei Jukku Kannon Gyo, just like we did tonight.
And I remember thinking, what the heck did I just say?
These names, Avalokiteshvara, Shariputra, and the way words are used, it just didn't make much sense to me.
Maybe some of you pondered the same questions.
If you've been around for a while, and you've taken Heart Sutra classes, and you know all this, just be patient tonight.
I titled the talk "Opening the Heart."
More accurate would be "the opening of the Heart Sutra," but I like "Opening the Heart," more poetic.
We all chanted these lines together tonight, and I hope that a few different commentaries might help, and that we might have a conversation after the talk.
It doesn't matter if you chanted the Heart Sutra tonight for the first time, or the hundredth, or the thousandth.
My idea was to provide some food for thought.
I'm more in the hundred-plus, thousand-plus category.
To me, the Heart Sutra has a purpose.
It represents a super-compressed list of Buddhist teachings.
With a couple of words, it embraces huge concepts and ideas.
It's a Buddhist teaching and contemplation manual.
It's not just something to be read or recited.
I have great hope that at some point you will make the Heart Sutra personal and relevant to you.
Make it yours.
Meditate on its meaning.
It does give us the heart essence, the perfection of wisdom or insight.
It doesn't give us all the details.
It's our job to fill those in over the years.
So I'm trying to say: really groove on the Heart Sutra.
It's difficult because so many things are just pointed at from a distance in the Sutra.
For example, the complete teaching of the Four Noble Truth and the Eightfold Path is in these words: no suffering, no cause, no cessation, no path.
The interesting thing is that it points at this fundamental teaching of Buddhism in those few words.
But what's even stranger is that at the same time, it denies it all.
No, no, no, no.
That's a really good point, and food for another talk.
I'm just using this as an example to demonstrate the compression that we see in this Sutra.
But onward with the subject.
I especially would like to bring up the boring parts.
Why?
Because unraveling the boring parts usually means unraveling the nuts and bolts, what really makes it work.
The basics.
I don't know about you, but I usually like to skip the basics.
I know this already.
So here's the opening of the Heart Sutra, which we just chanted.
*Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva, when deeply practicing prajnaparamita, clearly saw that all five aggregates are empty and thus relieved all suffering.
Shariputra, form does not differ from emptiness.
Emptiness does not differ from form.
Form itself is emptiness.
Emptiness itself form.
Sensations, perceptions, formations and consciousness are also like this.
Shariputra, all dharmas are marked by emptiness.
They neither arise nor cease, are neither defiled nor pure, neither increase nor decrease.*
Well, let's start out by taking a look at some individual words and phrases.
Please bear with me if you've heard all of this before.
Avalokiteshvara.
Avalokiteshvara is the Bodhisattva, the avatar, the saint of compassion.
Avalokiteshvara is compassion personified.
In a different religion, we might call him a patron saint.
On a side note, Avalokiteshvara in his original form in India was a male.
When Avalokiteshvara came to China, he became female and was now Kuan Yin, also known as Kannon or Kanseyon in Japan.
The next is prajnaparamita.
Prajna means wisdom or enlightenment.
Paramita means perfection.
So when we talk about prajnaparamita, it is the perfection of wisdom, and something about perfection.
This is a really horrible word in our day-to-day life.
Perfection is what keeps us away from contentment.
You know, I could do this a little better, and so on.
But to me, in this sense, it means that I continue to work on it, not with the intention to ever have it perfect, but to attain a contentment with this practice.
We could also say perfection of direct insight into the truth as taught by the Buddha, and it is a quality required to attain enlightenment.
I copied that somewhere, because I can't tell you a whole bunch about enlightenment.
So let's see.
The next phrase that would strike us as strange is the five aggregates.
When I first came, the five aggregates were still the five skandhas, which is more like the technical expression for it.
When we're done with the general overview, I'm going to jump back to the skandhas and explain a little more.
Then the Heart Sutra talks a lot about being empty.
So the logical question is: empty of what?
And we answer: empty of a separate, independent self.
Empty of weightiness, empty of burden, empty of boundary, empty of the big sack we schlep around through our lives that weighs us down and makes us do stupid things.
It's empty of all that.
Suffering, that's another one.
At some point when Buddhist literature was translated, someone made the unfortunate decision to translate the word dukkha as suffering.
One, it plays a really important role in Buddhism.
It's one of the three marks of existence, which are anatman, not self; anitya, impermanence; and dukkha, unease, dis-ease, discomfort, suffering.
And often in enlightened literature, such as we find on Facebook and Instagram, there are these lines: the Buddha says that life is suffering.
No, the Buddha didn't say that.
This is what the Buddha said.
*Birth is dukkha, aging is dukkha, illness is dukkha, death is dukkha, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are dukkha.
Association with the unbeloved is dukkha, separation from the loved is dukkha, not getting what is wanted is dukkha.
In conclusion, the five clinging aggregates are dukkha.*
Another word that doesn't happen in our regular vocabulary is Shariputra.
Shariputra was one of the main disciples of the Buddha.
The interesting thing is that Zen is a Mahayana Buddhist sect, and it's really interesting that in Mahayana Sutras, Shariputra is always the fall guy.
He's the one who doesn't get it.
Another one is Ananda.
But Shariputra is usually the one they pick on, and Ananda is the one who permanently doesn't get it.
I think that is somewhat unfortunate.
It's like the "my karate teacher can beat up your karate teacher" thing: our tradition of Buddhism is better than that old stuff.
So I would just ignore it.
I usually do, unless I speak up about it, because both Shariputra and Ananda are really dear to my heart, especially Ananda, because he never gets it and I never get it either.
So he gets a treatment that is, A, not historical, and B, unkind.
Then the next word is Dharma.
In our practice we encounter two dharmas.
One, with a capital D, is the teaching, the universal law, the word of the Buddha, however you want to put it.
The other one is the phenomena that are around us.

In Abhidharma, which is another theoretical piece of Buddhist writing, it is the smallest unit of experience that can happen, which is not very helpful to imagine, but I thought I'd bring it up anyway.
I thought it would be fun to now put this all together, as if we chanted a decoded Heart Sutra.

*Avalokiteshvara, who is the avatar of compassion, when deeply immersed in the practice of the perfection of wisdom, clearly saw that the five pillars that make us human have no independent self-existence.
They inter-are, depend, and rely on the rest of the universe, space, and time.
Thus Avalokiteshvara relieved all dis-ease and unsatisfactoriness.
He said, Shariputra, form does not differ from emptiness of a separate independent self.
Empty of weightiness, empty of burden, empty of boundary, emptiness does not differ from form.
Form itself is emptiness, emptiness itself form.
Sensations do not differ from emptiness.
Emptiness does not differ from sensations.
Perceptions do not differ from emptiness.
Emptiness does not differ from perceptions.
Formations do not differ from emptiness.
Emptiness does not differ from formation.
Consciousness does not differ from emptiness.
Emptiness does not differ from consciousness.
Shariputra, all forms and experiences are marked by being empty of a separate independent self.
They neither arise nor cease, and are neither defiled nor pure, neither increase nor decrease.*
I know this is not very changeable.
We can read all kinds of different scholars and teachers, and their commentaries are sometimes totally different.
That doesn't mean that one is wrong and the other one is right.
They did what I referenced early on in the talk: you need to make it yours.
You need to make it your understanding.
But they all point at the same heart.
So like I said, make it personal.
And now comes the big question with which I will end my talk: how will we unfold the heart of the Heart Sutra?
